item.title: Helen Chiang, Xbox’s first-ever chief operating officer (COO), is leaving Microsoft just three months after taking the job. Read more
item.description:
Helen Chiang, Xbox’s first-ever chief operating officer (COO), is leaving Microsoft just three months after taking the job.
According to The Verge, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma confirmed Chiang’s departure in an internal memo circulated on 23rd October.
"Helen Chiang is leaving Microsoft today. I'm grateful for her years of service and wish her well," Sharma wrote.
Sharma provided no details on why Chiang - who'd been at Microsoft for 21 years and had previously served as head of Minecraft - was leaving the company, only adding, "we'll share more on COO leadership as plans are finalised". It's thought her duties will be shared between other Xbox execs.
Sharma created the role in July as part of Xbox's massive "reset", saying it was needed to "work toward a shared goal, make the right tradeoffs, and get things done". It also came with 3200 layoffs and four studio departures in "most significant" Xbox restructuring in history.
Microsoft revealed that Psychonauts developer Double Fine, State of Decay studio Undead Labs, and South of Midnight developer Compulsion Games would go independent following negotiations, while Hellblade developer Ninja Theory is now likely to close after two acquisition deals fell through.
Arkane Lyon - the beloved immersive sim studio behind the likes of Dishonored and Deathloop - is the one still in limbo, and yesterday we learned it reportedly only has until November to find a buyer.

item.description:
Hello, it is me, your regular weekend host Mertie and I am here once again to guide you gently into Saturday with our usual feature What We've Been Playing, where we write a little about the games we've been, yes, playing. This week, Bertie - before fleeing for a well-deserved break and leaving me with the keys to the place - runs a one-on-one D&D game; Connor plays with his Moon Flesh in Warframe, and I've been serenely gallivanting over yonder hills.
But enough about us, what about you? What have you been playing this week? Do tell all! And don't forget we have an entire archive of previous What We've Been Playings for your leisurely perusal, just in case you forgot what you were playing a year or a month or a week ago.
I'm a little busy outside of work at the moment with rehearsals for a play I'm in (The Importance of Being Ernest), but I did find time for another Dungeons & Dragons first: a one-on-one game. I've been wanting to do one of these for a while, and, as I discovered recently, one-on-one games are a whole thing. Duets, they're called, rather poetically. You need to modify campaigns a bit to be playable this way, because most are designed for groups of four or five people, and you probably need to give a player a companion character as backup. But otherwise, it's totally doable. Some people make adventures exclusively for one-on-one games.
I ran a mini-adventure called D8 Night, created by the now-closed dice shop Dakota Irish. It's a nice, warm two-hour-or-so affair, where the player is caught in a time-stilled village and tasked by some magical mischief maker to retrieve the components of a romantic meal before being allowed to leave. It's a simple enough set-up, and as with a lot of things D&D, the set-up doesn't really matter so much as the playing of it and the unexpected things that happen. And unexpected things did happen. I played with my partner so I know her likes pretty well, I like to think - that's the attraction of a one-on-one set-up like this - but I didn't expect her to connect so strongly with some of the incidental characters. This resulted in entire areas being imagined-to-life that weren't written on paper. The imagination never ceases to amaze me.
Anyway, I'm off to Comic Con this weekend to celebrate my birthday - it'll be my birthday when you're reading this. I'm off to geek-out about Critical Role and watch the new Laika animated film, and to stuff my face with food.
I had a lovely time playing developer Funselektor's Art of Rally follow-up Over the Hill last week, roaming its beautifully stylised wilderness expanses in my cheerful 4x4 so I could write some words about it all. But it clearly got its hooks into me, and I went on to spend pretty much my entire Saturday just pootling around the Canadian Valhallas, the Algerian desert, thoroughly transfixed by the tranquil rhythms of it all.
It really is a game for the curious - and the infinitely patient. As the old meme goes: See that mountain?, you can climb it. Just be prepared for a lot of slow-going, a lot of trial-and-error, and a lot of determination. But while it should be frustrating, the opposite somehow ends up being true, and it's easy to feel at peace in this striking wilderness, guitars strumming gentle encouragement as you become one with the world.
You haven't experienced FOMO until you've experienced MMO do-this-or-you'll-never-be-able-to-do-it-again FOMO: The once-in-a-lifetime grinds, the cosmetics that may be vaguely impressive to onlookers in a decade's time, and the first-thing-in-the-morning, last-thing-at-night routines of logging on and doing busywork.
For those unaware, Warframe is currently bracing for a journey into a whole new galaxy. The trip requires fuel, but given we're talking about the big-red-number-loving, fashion-forward, weirdly wonderful Warframe here, this fuel isn't diesel. No, Warframe players in their thousands are currently shoving Moon Flesh into an alien grandma's mouth.
We're taking parts of Eris - a grim petri dish home to countless infested ghouls - and, fouler still, the Mesa warframe. Like a ripe cheese, its stink is what meemaw craves, and providing it brings great rewards. These include weapons and dead-handy consumables like Legendary Cores and Archon Shards, but perhaps more delectable are the cosmetics. Some must be unlocked through a community-wide effort, while others are available to buy with Moon Flesh from the jump. And, of course, once the event ends, these will never return. Never ever.
I've been waking up at 6am everyday and doing missions for this Moon Flesh, and I've been doing it before bed as well. I, like many hopeless MMO/-live service players, am petrified that something in the game may never be mine to hoard. It has cut into my gym time, my morning coffee time, and indeed my sleep time. I owe my recent spree of unsubtle yawns in morning team meetings to Warframe. That's either a glowing endorsement, or a sign I need to ease up on this stuff. Who knows?
Am I allowed two entries? I'm not actually sure, but Bertie's not here to stop me so... ALSO, I have found myself consumed by Switch Sports Resort this week in a way I absolutely wasn't expecting to be when I fired it up for review. In my head, Nintendo's long-running series has always very much been a party game first, and an engaging solo endeavour a distant second.
But Switch Sports Resort is a bit of a treasure, and I've been having a great time with it on my own: taking it online for a bit of ranked or casual play, working through some achievements, or just firing up one of its fantastic open-world sightseeing modes for a leisurely explore. I hope Nintendo's got some post-launch plans in the works, because I'd love for it to go a little bit harder with the open-world stuff, particularly where flying is concerned. But until then there's skateboarding, which is bloody brilliant, and I'm already craving more.

item.title: Legendary Nintendo developer Shigeru Miyamoto - who led development on classic games such as Super Mario 64 and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time - has argued that the rise of generative AI tools won't necessarily replace human talent. Read more
item.description:
Legendary Nintendo developer Shigeru Miyamoto - who led development on classic games such as Super Mario 64 and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time - has argued that the rise of generative AI tools won't necessarily replace human talent.
Next month, Shigeru Miyamoto will become the first ever video game developer to be awarded the Order of Culture by the Emperor of Japan, a hugely prestigious honour. But in a recent press conference dedicated to the award, he also shared some thoughts about gen-AI and its use in game production.
"Our generation lived through a period of rapid computer development - a time when tools were constantly evolving, moving from typewriters to word processors,” he said while speaking to the press, in quotes translated by VGC. Miyamoto argued that a designer's true capabilities "finally came to the fore" as technology advanced and was capable of handling more of what might be considered "labor", and a similar transition may take place with generative AI tech.
"While the act of creation is inherently satisfying, there's a danger: one might find satisfaction in the labor itself and mistakenly believe that a high-quality piece of work has been created," he added. If generative-AI software replaces more tasks involved in game production, human game devs might have "an opportunity to reflect on what's really important."
"Looking back at past designs, there are some that were created merely by copying and pasting. Yet, such work rarely stands the test of time; it lacks the individual’s particular design intention," Miyamoto continued. "Because the process relies on an individual's intent, with the computer serving as an assistant for the labor, I believe that even as technology continues to evolve, and even if AI were to eventually handle everything, there will always be a role left for us to play."
Masahiro Sakurai was a bit less optimistic about a potentially AI-first future than his peer. The Smash Bros. director recently said gen-AI tech might lead to a surge of unoriginal and unprofitable games, though it won't be able to replicate the creativity of humans.
Nintendo itself hasn't outright ruled out the possibility of using gen-AI tools in the future, but former Nintendo of America president Doug Bowser assured folks that the company's games would retain a "human touch" last year. "We still believe that what makes our games special is our developers, their artistic capabilities, their insight into how people play," Bowser said at the time.
Nintendo is somewhat at odds with several of its contemporaries when it comes to AI adoption, however. Square Enix CEO Takashi Kiryu previously said the company would be "aggressive in applying AI." Sega, Capcom, Level-5, Epic Games and a number of other high-profile game studios have admitted to using gen-AI in some form, as well. Xbox even opened an entire division seemingly dedicated to experimenting with the tech.

item.title: A deal between Netflix and Xbox has supposedly fallen through because of one minor quibble: Netflix wanted to adapt the console maker's games for $500m, not $800m. Read more
item.description:
A deal between Netflix and Xbox has supposedly fallen through because of one minor quibble: Netflix wanted to adapt the console maker's games for $500m, not $800m.
That's according to Puck News' Matt Belloni, who reports that Netflix offered Xbox $500m to exclusively licence the company's games and turn them into streamable films or TV shows for the next seven years.
Xbox CEO Asha Sharma and the division's business affairs team then responded with an eye-watering counter offer, according to the report. Xbox supposedly asked the streamer for $800m to sign off on the same deal.
Former Netflix CCO Bela Bajaria reportedly approached the game publisher first, but the executive's departure and Xbox's expensive counter offer led to the deal falling apart. Netflix CFO Spence Neumann was apparently one of the streamer's top heads who thought the deal wasn't worth the $800m price tag.
It's unclear which games would've been included in the film and TV deal considering multiple Xbox brands are already on their way to screens both big and small. Amazon is working to adapt Wolfenstein into a live-action series and will soon debut the third season of its acclaimed Fallout show, for example, while Paramount is turning Call of Duty into a blockbuster movie.
Netflix and Xbox are still working together on other projects, though. Animated shows based on Minecraft and Diablo are already in the works, as is a live-action Gears of War film. Blizzard Entertainment president Johanna Faries recently teased the crowd at BlizzCon 2026 by suggesting Overwatch and Warcraft could receive a similar treatment, too.
"We have received record-breaking interest in our IP," Xbox said in a statement to Puck News. "Netflix is a valued partner and we are excited for the forthcoming release of our Minecraft and Diablo animated series together, among other adaptations." The outlet claims Xbox is continuing to pursue smaller licensing deals.
Game adaptations are all the rage right now. This year's excellent Resident Evil reboot, Illuminations' Super Mario Bros duology, HBO's The Last of US, Amazon's Fallout and three live-action Sonic The Hedgehog films have found huge success - and encouraged practically every major studio to go hunting for their own game licenses. They're not all hits, however. This year's Street Fighter and Mortal Kombat 2 were released to a more tepid crowd.

item.description:
After getting caught up in Xbox CEO Asha Sharma's devastating layoffs and cuts earlier this year, Arkane Lyon - the beloved immersive sim studio behind the likes of Dishonored and Deathloop - reportedly only has until November to find a buyer. If the search fails, it will be shut down.
Arkane Lyon was one of a number of first-party studios reportedly facing closure ahead of Xbox's massive "reset" in July. However, when the layoffs were officially announced - bringing confirmation that 3,200 Xbox employees will eventually lose their jobs as part of the sweeping restructuring - Microsoft revealed Psychonauts developer Double Fine, State of Decay studio Undead Labs, and South of Midnight developer Compulsion Games would go independent following negotiations.
Hellblade studio Ninja Theory is now likely to close after two acquisition deals fell through, only leaving the fate of Arkane Lyon - a studio Microsoft acquired in 2021 when it purchased ZeniMax - uncertain. At the time, Xbox said it was "beginning required consultation with its Works Council to review potential strategic options" regarding Arkane, but little has been heard since.
Now, a report by French publication Le Monde (via Google Translate) has shed additional light on the studio's fate. Speaking to the publication, Printemps Écologique and the Video Game Workers’ Union (STJV) said Xbox management had informed Arkane Lyon it was facing closure on 16th July. As Le Monde notes, however, Microsoft's plan was complicated by French law, which requires a company with more than 1,000 employees to spend three months seeking a new buyer for any operational arm it plans to close. Only then, if no buyer is found, can it be shut down.
According to Le Monde, the search - alongside a consultation process and negotiations regarding an employment protection plan - began this summer, and the deadline to find a buyer for the studio is imminent, ending on 13th November. If the closure occurs, 217 workers could lose their jobs.
However, a union representative told the publication redundancy negotiations, which seemingly include efforts to get Arkane workers redeployed to other Microsoft studios, are going "badly", and that unions are trying to buy more time in the hope of saving the studio and its jobs. Reportedly, "several forms of takeover are being considered."
In response to the report, Microsoft did not confirm or deny Arkane's proposed closure, but told Le Monde, "We continue to explore various options for Arkane as part of the ongoing French consultation process". It also said it was "keeping the Social and Economic Committee and our employees informed." Internal documents seen by the publication say "the implementation of the plan [for the total and definitive cessation of the company's operations] is scheduled to begin at the end of 2026 and is expected to continue throughout the first quarter of 2027."
Amid all this turmoil, it's unclear what might happen to Arkane Lyon's current project, Marvel's Blade. In July, Xbox insisted "none of [its] first-party publicly announced games or projects" would be cancelled as part of Sharma's cuts, suggesting Blade - which hasn't been seen since its announcement in 2023 - was safe. Earlier this year, the game was rumoured to be dead, but a follow-up report from The Verge claimed that while it was "over-budget", it was now targeting a release in 2027 after an internal delay.
Earlier this month, Sharma insisted Xbox had "started to return to growth" following the company's sweeping cuts, but reports suggest three more rounds of layoffs are still to come, possibly starting before October is through.

item.title: After EA's sudden shutdown of developer BioWare, upcoming crossover items themed around Mass Effect appear to have been removed from Battlefield 6. Read more
item.description:
After EA's sudden shutdown of developer BioWare, upcoming crossover items themed around Mass Effect appear to have been removed from Battlefield 6.
When Battlefield 6's Season Five dropped earlier this month, many eager fans spotted that a collection of Mass Effect items had sneakily been added to the shooter's cosmetic menus, but were still unavailable to unlock or buy. The cosmetics included a little Normandy ship charm that dangled off weapons, some weapons that wouldn't look out of place in Mass Effect's sci-fi world and a few N7 tags. (Good spot, IGN!)
DICE has quietly removed all 'Mass Effect' cosmetics from #Battlefield6 after BioWare closure. Player card backgrounds, weapon skins, weapon charms, weapon stickers, sprays, soldier patches... everything. https://t.co/8KkjOm8nX2
With N7 Day right around the corner - slated for the 7th of November, as per usual - series fans reckoned the items would serve to celebrate the series' annual tradition and perhaps herald more news of Mass Effect 5. Those hopes were short-lived, sadly - developer BioWare is no more and the next Mass Effect game has been cancelled.
Following the shock closure, all Mass Effect items have seemingly been scrubbed from Battlefield 6's menus. Players spotted their absence in no time and shared the news online.
Battlefield 6's recent Dead Space crossover event already invited lots of divided opinions, with some players upset that the widely loved horror series is stuck in limbo while EA uses it to feed its live-service machine. Perhaps pulling a similar trick with Mass Effect - by celebrating N7 Day despite the series' uncertain future - would've simply poured salt onto a freshly opened wound. Although, the cosmetics were seemingly finished and ready to go.
In its announcement memo, EA said it was "making deliberate choices to align talent and investment where we see the greatest opportunities for players and long-term growth" - hence the decision to lay off 400 workers and cut BioWare entirely. The games industry has since mourned the loss of a beloved, long-standing role-playing institution.
A former BioWare dev recently claimed Mass Effect 5 would've borrowed from Baldur's Gate 3 and The Witcher to deliver unprecedented player choice. We'll never know for sure what BioWare would've cooked up, but a leaked trailer for Mass Effect Universe gives us a taste - a small, bittersweet, neon-drenched taste.
EA itself was recently taken private by the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, Jared Kushner's private equity group Affinity Partners and Silver Lake in a $55bn leveraged buyout.

item.title: Modern Warfare 4's DMZ extraction shooter mode has only been out for two days - and only for those who pre-ordered the game - but already players are up in arms over a particular trait that allows competitors to revive themselves after being killed. Read more
item.description:
Modern Warfare 4's DMZ extraction shooter mode has only been out for two days - and only for those who pre-ordered the game - but already players are up in arms over a particular trait that allows competitors to revive themselves after being killed.
That trait is called Possum, and is one of the many abilities players can unlock as they level up their operators. How it works is this: if the trait is active, you're given the option, once per match, to revive yourself on command when killed. Doing so places you in a Last Stand state, and you'll need to pick yourself up from this vulnerable downed position to continue playing. All together, getting back into the firefight from dead takes around 10 uninterrupted seconds. You also lose any loot you've gathered when you revive - so you're back to square one.
It goes without saying that the ability to come back to life at all in an extraction shooter is a bold addition to DMZ. There doesn't seem to be a great way to see if a dead opponent has it, meaning every player you kill could come back for revenge later in the match when your guard is down. It doesn't take long to unlock either! If you focus your operator progression solely on the Warfighter path, Possum can be unlocked in a handful of hours. As such, it's likely someone in a DMZ match will be ready to pounce. And to say Possum is proving divisive among Call of Duty players would be an understatement.
"Possum is garbage and needs to be deleted ASAP," pdmaloney94 wrote on the DMZ subreddit. This mechanic breaks DMZ in my opinion and severely takes the stakes out of [matches]. After fully killing a team we now have to babysit their corpses until we can confirm that they returned to the lobby? Who on earth thought this was a good idea to implement into an extraction shooter?"
That sentiment was mirrored by other players too. "I just clutched a 1v3 in the underground mall, go to revive my teammate before looting anyone, and the first person I killed is laying in the corner and kills me, "SkinDiesel wrote. "Why the f**k would they add a perk like that to an extraction shooter? I get the self-revives and tourniquets, but reviving yourself from death for free every single game is diabolical."
Some players pushed back, however, offering a more measured evaluation of Possum and some strategies to counter it. "Just move on and they won’t catch you because they have no loot to pursue," suggested cleppingout. Wilus82 brought up an interesting idea too: "I was reading that people were saying to put trip mines or land mines on their bodies."
Already, prominent Call of Duty YouTubers are decrying the trait. Phixate lambasted it as "completely broken", while Wynn-Gaming called Possum "crazy" - the trait drawing criticism largely due to its potential impact on team-vs-team gunfights. After all, pushing toward a team once you take down one of their members and thin out the ranks is a strategy as old as time. If that apparent numbers advantage suddenly evaporates mid-conflict, it's potentially a big deal.
My take? I hope Possum doesn't get nerfed, at least for a few weeks. Let it ride. Already we're seeing the way it's encouraging players to adopt interesting new strategies, and two days isn't nearly enough time to determine whether the trait is genuinely broken. Let the meta game settle, allow people to push it to its limits, then, if it remains a problem by December, call pest patrol on the possum.
DMZ's new trait isn't the only thing raising eyebrows, of course.. Players have been spawning in the middle of roads and immediately getting run over, which is hilarious. It'll be interesting to see what else emerges when the wider populace gains access later today.

item.description:
It's been 19 years since the release of Half-Life 2: Episode 2, and yet the ceaseless clamour for a Valve game with a number '3' in its title continues. And following a swell of reports suggesting Half-Life 3 isn't just real, its development is well underway, a Valve developer has gone and sent the internet a-chatter all over again by publicly, albeit accidentally, referencing its codename during a livestream.
Valve's first attempt at releasing a Half-Life game with a '3' in its name would have been the ill-fated Half-Life 2: Episode 3, which was abandoned - despite Valve previously announcing it as part of a planned trilogy - sometime around 2009. After that, the studio seemingly had a crack at making a full-blown sequel, with Valve boss Gabe Newell confirming a few years back that Half-Life 3 had been in development around 2013/2014, but was ultimately scrapped because it was built on the unfinished Source 2 engine.
Sometime in 2021, however, dataminers began to notice something interesting: repeated references to a project codenamed "HLX" in Valve-related files. Inevitably, this led to a frenzy of speculation that Valve might finally be reviving its long-anticipated first-person shooter sequel. And evidence has seemingly continued to amass over time. In 2024, for instance, Valve insider Tyler McVicker shared some of his datamined findings, claiming what he'd found pointed to a new "fully-fledged Half-Life game" - a claim coinciding with a leak from an actor likely involved in the project.
It all reached something of a crescendo when McVicker released a new video last year suggesting the rumoured Half-Life 3 was now "playable, end-to-end", and claimed it could even release before 2025 was through. Fans, meanwhile, did some sleuthing and concluded Half-Life 3 would likely launch in either November or December last year. All of this, clearly, did not come to pass, and the Half-Life 3 hype has died down a little since then. And yet here we are again, with the latest twist in the saga being a public reference to the codenamed 'HLX' by a Valve developer, albeit seemingly accidentally.
Let us jump to a recent GameSoundCon Q&A panel (promptly clipped and shared by McVicker again), in which Valve's music designer Mike Morasky spent some time discussing the audio work on the company's games. "Deadlock has their own version of HDR," Morasky explained, "HLX has its own version, and so on and so forth." Midway through the sentence, Morasky seems to taper off, as if immediately realising the error of his ways. Soon after, Valve sound designer David Feise appears to lean over and whisper "nice work", which some have understandably taken to be sarcasm.
So what does all this tell us? Not a lot, really, beyond the fact it suggests HLX is a thing (which we mostly already knew) and that it's still being worked on. Morasky's framing would, however, also suggest that whatever HLX is, it's a standalone project, and one requiring music at that. So I guess those Half-Life 3 dreams can live on for another day. The only question remaining, which will arrive first: Half-Life 3 or the heat death of the sun?

item.title: Chinese action game Phantom Blade Zero already appears to be outperforming massive games like Gears of War: E-Day and Control Resonant on Steam, despite still being days from release. Read more
item.description:
Chinese action game Phantom Blade Zero already appears to be outperforming massive games like Gears of War: E-Day and Control Resonant on Steam, despite still being days from release.
That's according to sales data scrutinised by Alinea Analytics head of market analysis Rhys Elliott, who posted their findings on LinkedIn. Based on Elliott's estimates, Phantom Blade Zero has already sold 500,000 copies on Steam through pre-orders, bringing in roughly $24m in revenue ahead of its launch next week. Elliott noted the figures meant Phantom Blade Zero was "outperforming" Gears of War: E-Day and Control Resonant on Steam at the time of writing, and that China is currently its top market.
Other interesting tidbits include the fact that Phantom Blade Zero has also generated a lofty 2.5m Steam wishlists. According to Elliott, 41 percent of players who've wishlisted the game have also played Black Myth Wukong, while 38 percent of them have played Elden Ring and 28 percent played Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice.
It's an impressive start for Phantom Blade Zero on PC, and Elliott goes on to say that "pre-launch signals" point to the game being popular on PS5 too. He even goes as far as to suggest it has the "potential to be one of the year's breakout single-player hits."
These figures emerge at a time China's games industry is enjoying a boom, and an increasing number of releases from Chinese developers are launching to critical and commercial success worldwide. Phantom Blade Zero has all the signs of becoming another hit it launches for PS5 and PC on 28th October.

item.title: An internal trailer for the cancelled Mass Effect game that was in-development at BioWare prior to its closure this week has appeared online. It's confirmed to be real, too, amid some initial suspicions it may have been an AI generated fake. Read more
item.description:
An internal trailer for the cancelled Mass Effect game that was in-development at BioWare prior to its closure this week has appeared online. It's confirmed to be real, too, amid some initial suspicions it may have been an AI generated fake.
The trailer was intended for internal use, and was created for EA leadership rather than the public. It starts with a short message: "The following is in-engine footage from our small team. It uses our pre-production assets."
The trailer shows us our first (and likely only) look at Mass Effect Universe, an entirely new entry following the adventures of a new protagonist. We see them navigate the galaxy in their own ship with a new crew of various known races including a Krogan, and get into fights using guns and biotics. There's some quick cuts to a saucy romance scene, a tense standoff with weapons drawn, and a mysterious creature being researched in a big test tube. We also see a returning character from the original trilogy - Liara - make an appearance near the end of the trailer before a big bar fight kicks off.
When first released, scepticism around whether this trailer was real naturally was present given the prevalence of AI, however IGN quickly verified its validity. In addition, Bloomberg's Jason Schrier went on to corroborate the trailer's authenticity on his personal BlueSky account.
We know very little about this game aside from this trailer. According to a former BioWare employee, Mass Effect Universe would have learned from Baldur's Gate 3 and The Witcher to deliver "a level of autonomy and choice that no other game has." The game would have also seemingly "remained true" to the original trilogy.
Reactions from this trailer are bittersweet, given the reality that the 50 developers working on Mass Effect Universe have recently lost their jobs as part of EA's layoffs which impacted 400 employees across the company. "A spy thriller is such a cool concept for a re-entry to the series," wrote Reddit user Harrywilko. "Man, I'm just so sad and angry." User TerraxFormer shared similar sentiments, writing: "God this makes me even more distraught lol. I know a trailer is not an indication of how good it would have been but I was looking forward to this damn game so much."
The EA job cuts, which took place only a few months after Saudi Arabia's $55bn leveraged buyout of the company, also hit developers at Respawn, Maxis, Full Circle, EA Motive, and other EA-owned studios. While such cuts were anticipated by experts given EA's new debt obligations, the news of BioWare's closure nonetheless drew out many messages of sympathy and anger from across the industry.
It's hardly a silver lining, given we saw this unfinished trailer while we all said a sad farewell to BioWare. But at least those staff can know they were onto something that could have been great.

item.title: Masahiro Sakurai has spoken about the pitfalls of generative AI use in game development, saying that while he believes the technology will result in a surge of unoriginal video games, human creativity - such as that shown by designers like Ico's Fumito Ueda - can't be replicated. item.description:
Masahiro Sakurai has spoken about the pitfalls of generative AI use in game development, saying that while he believes the technology will result in a surge of unoriginal video games, human creativity - such as that shown by designers like Ico's Fumito Ueda - can't be replicated.
In an interview with Japanese news outlet Denfaminicogamer, Sakurai was asked about his time judging for the Game Designers Awards (a role he recently retired from) and his thoughts on the massive increase of game releases since the awards began. In 2010, 275 games were published on Steam, whereas more than 19,000 released this year.
"19,000 is amazing, but I think that number will increase even more from now on," Sakurai said (as translated from Japanese using Google Translate). "I'm sure of it. That's because AI will increase the number. However, I think most of them will become 'unprofitable titles'. There are too many to keep track of, and it's impossible to understand them all.
"When it comes to things created with AI... or things mass-produced with poor quality, I think most of them will simply be reproductions of systems seen in various other games. I think there are already a lot of those now."
Sakurai then spoke about a recent (and lovely) release called Librarian: Tidy Up the Arcane Library!, which challenges players to organise books on shelves, and pointed to other puzzle games with similarly simple premises, such as finding a needle in a haystack or organising a supermarket. These kinds of games, he suggested, will be very easy for AI to replicate.
We've already seen this happen, of course. Needle in a Haystack Simulator, for example - which asks players to find a needle buried among 5 million pieces of hay - went viral thanks to its absurd yet compelling premise. Following its surge in popularity, copies were quickly created, prompting Needle in a Haystack developer Studio Bitdot to plop a bright red "original" tag on its Steam artwork.
But Sakurai continued, saying generative AI may become powerful enough to replicate more complicated games, like acclaimed designer Fumito Ueda's Ico or Shadow of the Colossus. However, he emphasised that Ueda's future games will be "something that AI simply cannot replicate ... What kind of artistic style will his future works possess? That's something only he can create. I think that's where human creativity lies."
"Basically, AI refers to things that have been created so far, but it can't refer to things that haven't been created before," Sakurai elaborated. "I think this is true not only for AI, but for various kinds of creative works as well.
"I wouldn't go so far as to call them 'pioneers', but rather people who forge their own path... people who understand and can create their own unique flavour... will become increasingly important from now on. I think this is especially true in an era of mass production and low-quality goods."
Quickly made AI games have become an increasing presence in the games industry of late. Valve's current Steam Next Fest features more than double the number of demos compared to last year, due in part to the influx of 'AI slop'. Some indie developers have even pulled planned demos and playtests out of fear their games might be copied by AI before they're properly released.

item.title: Oof. I expected this day to come but the news has left me winded nonetheless; BioWare, the creator of so many beloved role-playing series and games - Mass Effect, Dragon Age, Baldur's Gate, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic - has been closed. EA decided it had no place for it under its new Saudi and private investment ownership. So Mass Effect 5 has been canned, and a studio that helped shape an industry and popularise role-playing games over the course of 31 years is no more. Read more
item.description:
Oof. I expected this day to come but the news has left me winded nonetheless; BioWare, the creator of so many beloved role-playing series and games - Mass Effect, Dragon Age, Baldur's Gate, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic - has been closed. EA decided it had no place for it under its new Saudi and private investment ownership. So Mass Effect 5 has been canned, and a studio that helped shape an industry and popularise role-playing games over the course of 31 years is no more.
But it's a shock rather than a surprise. BioWare's days were numbered after the fizzle of Dragon Age: The Veilguard, although really, the studio was rocked long before then. The twin blows of Mass Effect: Andromeda in 2017 and Anthem in 2019 left it reeling, and even had Anthem been a success, BioWare would be irrevocably changed by it. We know all this. We've pored over BioWare's many shifts and misfires countless times over the years. Why? Because of how much BioWare has come to mean to so many of us.
There are distinct BioWare eras, and the early era unquestionably belongs to Baldur's Gate. As a series, it's not only directly responsible for the existence of Baldur's Gate 3, it's arguably responsible for the success of computer role-playing games (CRPGS) as a whole. BioWare created the Infinity Engine, you see, which characterised RPGs of the era. Black Isle used it to make Icewind Dale and Planescape: Torment (a game you can probably trace the much-loved Disco Elysium's lineage back to, with its deep, philosophical ways), not to mention that Fallout: New Vegas studio Obsidian Entertainment grew out of Black Isle. Baldur's Gate was also the first game The Witcher 3 developer CD Projekt Red would distribute in its early days - a licence without which it might not exist.
At the end of this CRPG era, BioWare released Neverwinter Nights. It was a game intended to be a total adaptation of Dungeons & Dragons, in that it not only offered a D&D adventure to play but a toolset to make your own campaigns with. That included a unique Dungeon Master system, whereby players could dynamically spawn enemies and offer guidance, just like a DM might in a live tabletop game. Larian tried a similar thing in Divinity: Original Sin 2, though we haven't seen many other games attempt it since - not unless you count BioWare's cancelled 4v1 game Shadow Realms, that is. With its user-generated content, player-run servers, and DM mode, Neverwinter Nights was ahead of its time, and it's still played to this day.
Onwards, and we race into BioWare's console era, to the creation of games that reverberate with influence even now. Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic - which gave Obsidian crucial work in making a sequel - and then Jade Empire, the Wushu RPG. Jade Empire didn't make much of an impact but during its promotion, BioWare provided CD Projekt Red with free E3 stand space to show its new game - a certain The Witcher - which was built on Neverwinter Nights' Aurora engine. "BioWare has been a massive part of CDPR history," CDPR joint-CEO Michał Nowakowski acknowledged on X following BioWare's closure.
Yet, all of this was really a precursor to the game and series BioWare would become best known for: Mass Effect. This sci-fi space opera trilogy took the template BioWare had been honing in previous games - party-based adventures featuring emotional storytelling and romanceable companions - and bedazzled a mainstream console audience with it. I remember going from being one of the only people in the Eurogamer office who knew or cared about BioWare - I literally ran home from the office to play Mass Effect 1 when it came out - to being one of its many admirers when Mass Effect 2 arrived. That game changed everything, and I'm amazed by the influence it still has to this day. As one small example, Gareth Damian Martin, creator of the widely acclaimed Citizen Sleeper series, counts Mass Effect 2 among their favourite games.
At the same time, there was Dragon Age - a series I adore but which struggled to find an identity over the years. Its beloved debut, Dragon Age: Origins, was a callback to Baldur's Gate; Dragon Age 2 was a rushed attempt at ensnaring a console audience; Dragon Age: Inquisition got caught straddling a new console hardware generation, and was bloated by its open-world RPG ambitions. As for its most recent entry... I've written a lot about Dragon Age: The Veilguard. Dragon Age has an uneven legacy, undoubtedly, but I say all this with love: it's probably the game series I feel closest to.
I'm also purposefully overlooking some other things - the Sonic RPG BioWare made! Not to mention the colossal MMO project Star Wars: The Old Republic, which was the reason we never got another single-player Knights of the Old Republic game. I remember interviewing BioWare doctor-founders Greg Zeschuk and Ray Muzyka at EGX 2011 before they announced the release date; it was a different era indeed. But the point of this potted history is simple: BioWare has been around for a very long time and made many games that mean many different things to many different people.
You could easily ask whether The Witcher series would exist without BioWare. It's not a stretch to say Larian wouldn't have had the breakout success it has without the brand power of Baldur's Gate. Equally, games like Exodus and The Expanse: Osiris Reborn probably wouldn't exist without Mass Effect as a template (Exodus even has notable former BioWare people working on it). And Casey Hudson's new Star Wars: Fate of the Old Republic game is a spiritual successor to Knights of the Old Republic.
Widen that further and would we have romance in role-playing games if it weren't for BioWare? Would we have as many party-based adventures with an emphasis on companions if it weren't for BioWare? Would we have a focus on good and evil influences, webs of choice and consequence, cinematic dialogue sequences? Would we have carried-over save games? Widen that further still: would as many people care about role-playing games if it weren't for BioWare? It wasn't the only studio doing these things, and maybe they would have materialised as strongly anyway, but BioWare established a template that became synonymous with RPGs.
And that word "care" is important, because I've always found the amount of withering scrutiny BioWare faced when announcing or releasing a game brutal - and at times, unfair. Though, I understand where it comes from. Consider the backlash to Mass Effect Andromeda for example: really, it existed because of the love for and expectations set by the Mass Effect trilogy. Or the backlash to various Dragon Age games: beyond the outrage bait of the culture war, it existed in part because the series kept changing and was no longer a CRPG. Even the backlash faced by Anthem came from a place of love, because people didn't want a Destiny game from BioWare, they wanted a BioWare game.
People wouldn't care if BioWare didn't matter to them, which is why it's been so hard to watch the studio be thrown around by EA's whims and trend-chasing over the years. Would BioWare really have embarked on an enormously expensive MMO, in SWTOR, had EA not wanted a World of Warcraft killer? Would BioWare really have decided to throw everything at Anthem had EA not wanted a game to rival Destiny? The game apparently never never had a single, unifying vision - but the flashiness of its flying won over boardrooms. What would Dragon Age 4 have been like had EA not scrapped the original 'Morrison' idea for a live service game - a pivot that resulted in the departure of long-time Dragon Age creative director Mike Laidlaw? In short: what would BioWare have made had EA not so heavily interfered?
Would BioWare co-founders Greg Zeschuk and Ray Muzyka have been able to hold off EA's execs and advances if they'd stuck around? I expect EA itself was partly one of the reasons they didn't. Really we have only what-ifs and assumptions, and it doesn't change where we are now. It doesn't change the fact that this isn't the ending BioWare deserved, and our thoughts are with everyone immediately affected by the studio's closure.
But hold for a moment and consider what we've had. Consider the reason why you're reading this at all: because BioWare means something to you. Because at some point, you played a BioWare game you connected with, presumably on a deep and emotional enough level that you began to care. Maybe it was many BioWare games; maybe it was a few. Whatever the number, whatever the game, it meant BioWare got through. And this was one of the few studios capable of that, at reflecting our humanity back at us and making us care. BioWare was a studio of stories, and its own story is worth celebrating too. As sad as it is to reach its end.

item.title: Multiple games - including Final Fantasy 14 and Umamusume: Pretty Derby - have faced outages and other issues following this week's discovery of a serious PHP vulnerability. Read more
item.description:
Multiple games - including Final Fantasy 14 and Umamusume: Pretty Derby - have faced outages and other issues following this week's discovery of a serious PHP vulnerability.
This vulnerability could potentially result in substantial security breaches for the massive number of websites and applications built using the PHP programming language. As a result, it was advised that online services built upon it should be taken offline until a fix could be distributed and applied. Inevitably, games were caught up.
An official post made to the Final Fantasy 14 lodestone website informed users that security "enhancements" were being made to the MMO's patch servers. As a result, new logins were temporarily disabled until the updates could be completed. While logins have since been turned back on, the server back-up feature for user's save data remains offline.
Horse racing gacha game Umamusume: Pretty Derby, meanwhile, was taken offline completely. As its server-side infrastructure uses PHP, a sudden maintenance outage was put in place - though its developer assured players no exploitation of the security vulnerability had occurred. Right now, Japanese and global servers are back online, with a compensatory package of in-game currency being sent to all players.
Path of Titans, an in-beta dinosaur MMO (which sounds awesome by the way) is still down as of writing. In an announcement made to its official X account, developer Alderon Games explained the MMOand its website had been taken down for up to three days as a precautionary measure. Players were also assured no data had been compromised.
One hopes the chaos is largely over now a fix is in circulation. But even if it is, the fact that so many services all across the globe - far beyond the games industry - have rushed to protect the sanctity of their data and that of their users speaks to the seriousness of the situation. Take a moment to thank the tech heads out there who may have had to work around the clock to get this sorted.

item.title: EA has closed its longtime studio partner BioWare, the iconic development house behind Mass Effect and Dragon Age, impacting around 50 staff who were in pre-production on the next Mass Effect game. In the aftermath of EA's decision, one of those affected has shared a little about the project, claiming it would have featured unprecedented levels of player freedom and choice reactivity. Read more
item.description:
EA has closed its longtime studio partner BioWare, the iconic development house behind Mass Effect and Dragon Age, impacting around 50 staff who were in pre-production on the next Mass Effect game. In the aftermath of EA's decision, one of those affected has shared a little about the project, claiming it would have featured unprecedented levels of player freedom and choice reactivity.
Tony de Waal, a BioWare veteran who has worked on previous Mass Effect and Dragon Age games, offered a rare look behind the scenes at what the team was attempting. In a LinkedIn post (via PC Gamer), de Waal suggested the studio wanted to surpass the acclaimed work of the role-playing giants at Baldur's Gate 3 studio Larian and CD Projekt Red, maker of The Witcher and Cyberpunk.
"I was one of the lucky ones who stayed with BioWare to start on the next Mass Effect, where I believe we were making something special: a level of autonomy and choice that no other game has been able to match," de Waal wrote. "We saw what Larian and CD Projekt were bringing to the table with their latest offerings, and started down a path to bring Mass Effect to the next level while remaining true to the trilogy," he added.
The veteran cinematics lead sadly didn't offer any examples of what that could've looked like in-game, but given previous Mass Effect games have incorporated a great deal of player freedom, the idea of a sequel that builds on that - while incorporating modern techniques from CDPR and Larian - would certainly have been exciting.
"I'm sad you won't ever get to see what we were cooking, and sad for the small, talented group of devs who were all punching above their weight to make something special," de Waal continued. "Please consider those who stayed with BioWare until the very end. They are truly some of the most talented people I've had the pleasure of working with throughout my career."
BioWare's closure feels sudden; it was only a year ago the studio stressed its new Mass Effect game remains in development. At the time, EA's private acquisition had just been announced. The $55bn sale has since been approved, freeing EA to start making cuts many suspected were coming.
More broadly, the move also signals an end to EA's interest in developing deep role-playing games. Outside of its sports and shooter series, EA's non-casual projects are an unannounced Star Wars Jedi sequel, and the Marvel's Iron Man game we've yet to see.

item.title: Marvel's Wolverine may not have had the best critical reception, but that clearly didn't discourage consumers. The action-adventure from Marvel's Spider-Man studio Insomniac has topped US video game sales in September, despite releasing exactly halfway through the month. Read more
item.description:
Marvel's Wolverine may not have had the best critical reception, but that clearly didn't discourage consumers. The action-adventure from Marvel's Spider-Man studio Insomniac has topped US video game sales in September, despite releasing exactly halfway through the month.
That's according to market analysis firm Circana, which noted Wolverine's success includes digital sales and those made at retail. It was such a hit that, as Circana analyst Mat Piscatella wrote, the game delivered "the highest launch month dollar sales" a Sony-published game has seen since Helldivers 2, which released in February 2024. It is worth noting, however, that Helldivers 2 launched on PC alongside PlayStation 5, while Wolverine is a PS5 exclusive. Additionally, Helldivers 2 had a much lower price of $40 compared to Wolverine's $70, meaning the former sold more copies to arrive at a similar point.
Wolverine seemingly helped boost PS5 sales, too, as the console saw a massive 43 percent uptick in dollar sales compared to the same period last year, though some of that is owed to its higher price now compared to then. In fact, PS5 led the month in both unit sales (up 22 percent from last year) and dollar sales across consoles. Switch 2 unit sales fell by 14 percent and Xbox by 27 percent - according to Circana, that means Xbox unit sales dropped to their lowest ever in a September, claiming the record from September 2025.
September, of course, was one of the busiest months for games this year, and that was reflected in the top-ten, which saw eight new releases - including The Blood of Dawnwalker, Onimusha: Way of the Sword, Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve, Switch 2-exclusive Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave, and PC-exclusive Wardogs. Also among those was NBA 2K27, which, despite failing to claim the top spot in September, surprisingly managed to dethrone Resident Evil Requiem to become the best-selling game this year so far - a record it surely can't hold on to for long with GTA 6 on the horizon.
Circana's most interesting report this year is undoubtedly going to be November's, when GTA 6 arrives, but October's should also be eye-opening, because it's Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's release month, the other major release of 2026.

item.title: Following the sudden closure of Bioware last night, people from across the games industry have shared their sympathies for those employees losing their jobs, and said farewell to one of the most influential RPG developers of all time. Read more
item.description:
Following the sudden closure of Bioware last night, people from across the games industry have shared their sympathies for those employees losing their jobs, and said farewell to one of the most influential RPG developers of all time.
The reactions come in many forms, with BioWare staff throughout the years looking back on their time at the studio and thanking their peers and fans for support. Game developers from other studios have paid tribute too, sharing their own tales of how Bioware impacted their careers.
"As much as it's not really a surprise," former Dragon age lead writer David Gaider on Bluesky, "especially given the industry right now coupled with the Saudi sale, the news today still made me sad ... BioWare joins other great studios of the past, with a legacy that will not soon be forgotten."
Former Knights of the Old Republic and Dragon Age lead James Ohlen also paid tribute to the studio, writing: "BioWare is closing. My 22 years there made me the man I am. The people affected today are some of the best RPG developers in the world. If you're hiring writers, designers, artists or engineers, start with them. Former BioWare folks: if an intro from me would help, reach out."
"This is sad news on multiple fronts," former Mass Effect boss and one-time BioWare general manager Casey Hudson added on X, "for those of us who worked there, for our friends and colleagues at BioWare who are impacted, and for fans who were looking forward to the next Mass Effect adventure.
"I started my career at BioWare and will forever be grateful to the founders, Greg and Ray, for inviting me to join in BioWare's legendary journey. Its legacy will live on through those who were part of it and continue to create games through a passion for unforgettable stories, worlds and characters."
"Remember BioWare is 100% owned by EA,” said Mark Darrah, former Dragon Age and Anthem executive producer in a YouTube video. “EA owns all the IPs. They own Dragon Age, they own Mass Effect, they own Jade Empire. That doesn’t change the situation, really, at all. [...] Now, there’s nobody working on a [BioWare] game, or games, within the EA organization, and chances are there never will be, which might make them more likely to sell off those IPs. But it might also make them more likely to just try to forget that they ever existed and bury them in the vault."
Trick Weekes, former narrative designer on the Mass Effect and Dragon Age series, posted a video from Mass Effect 3's Citadel DLC, in which Commander Shepard and their crew say a sombre farewell, while actor Mark Meer, the voice of male Shepard, shared his condolences and thanks with BioWare staff past and present.
Michael Gamble, who served as project director on the now-cancelled Mass Effect 5 until yesterday's layoffs also took to social media, thanking people for their support during his 17 years at the company, saying it "has meant everything to me."
While BioWare's closure prompted many studio alumni to share their thoughts, an outpouring of support and mourning came from outside the company too. "This is not something I ever expected to see," Swen Vincke, CEO of Baldur's Gate 3 developer Larian, wrote on social media. "Larian and Bioware started their trajectories in the games industry at the same time and Bioware led the way in making RPGs big. It's almost unimaginable that we're now entering an era where the name BioWare won't show up anymore when discussing upcoming RPGs. What a loss for all of us."
CD Projekt Red co-studio head Michał Nowakowski also recalled how important BioWare was to the Polish studio. "Bioware has been a massive part of CDPR history," he wrote. "We befriended them when localising and selling Baldur’s Gate games in Poland, Czech, and Slovakia. And later they were [a] great help when lending us their engine for Witcher 1, sharing their wisdom and even giving us a spot at their booth at E3. I had [the] pleasure to visit them a few times in Edmonton and also host them in our Warsaw office. Very sad for the people affected, but also sad to see a legendary brand go down. Not a great day in the games industry."
"Thank you for all the games. Thank you for the many hours of gameplay. Thank you for all the stories . You can be damned proud of what you achieved. I hope you all land well."
Nowakowski was joined by his peer Paweł Sasko, associate director of CD Projekt's upcoming Cyberpunk sequel, who revealed the importance of BioWare's games on his own career: "Baldur's Gate 1 and 2 shaped my imagination and the desire to create games. I would have never been here without BioWare igniting the fire in my heart. It inspired me, formed me, enriched my imagination, and for that I will be forever grateful. I will always remember you."
Dave Gilbert, founder of Old Skies and The Blackwell Legacy studio Wadjet Eye Games, similarly spoke of BioWare's impact on his career: "Eff me. Not Bioware, too. This one hurts more than most. I can't think of a studio that has had a bigger influence on me than this one. My dream was to be like them. I'll never stop feeling angry when studios with tremendous legacies just get bought and killed off for parts."
Some too had harsh words for EA and those behind Bioware's closure, alongside sympathy for those affected. Legendary immersive sim developer Warren Spector, for instance, decried the fact the development team had now been left "out in the cold with so many others."
"BioWare is more than just another studio," he continued. "For decades it’s played a central role in the history of our medium. They, for many years, as effectively as any studio, married art and commerce. Their work changed things. This is such bad news, such a devastating historic event all I can say is that it’s utter bullshit. Anyone who participated in this travesty should be ashamed.
"Actually, maybe all of the people who participated — the folks in suits (real or virtual) should lose their damn jobs. I ask them to ponder this: What do you contribute to gaming? What price do you pay for failure? I’d love to see THEM on the unemployment line instead of the people who do real work. Why is it always the do-ers and makers who pay the price? Someone explain that to me!"
Following news of BioWare's closure, EA confirmed other sweeping changes across the company, which will result in a total of 400 job cuts. While it did not explicitly name the other studios impacted by the move, employees have already started posting on social media, revealing the likes of Respawn, Maxis, Full Circle, EA Motive, and Ripple Effect have all been impacted. The layoffs come after EA was fully acquired by a consortium made up of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, investment firm Silver Lake, and private equity company Affinity Partners for $55bn earlier this year.
Eurogamer wishes all those impacted by the layoffs the very best for the future.

item.title: EA announced overnight it's closing Mass Effect and Dragon Age studio BioWare in a new round of cuts that include the elimination of 400 roles across the publisher. But while it confirmed BioWare's 50 workers are affected, and that Skate studio Ripple Effect was being downsized, it did not say where the other 350 job cuts would come from. Read more
item.description:
EA announced overnight it's closing Mass Effect and Dragon Age studio BioWare in a new round of cuts that include the elimination of 400 roles across the publisher. But while it confirmed BioWare's 50 workers are affected, and that Skate studio Ripple Effect was being downsized, it did not say where the other 350 job cuts would come from.
Now, however, new information has emerged revealing The Sims studio Maxis, Battlefield support studio Ripple Effect, and EA Motive are all impacted by layoffs, alongside Full Circle and BioWare. That's according to Vertical Slice, citing an "anonymous source" supported by corroborating information on LinkedIn.
Maxis senior director Anna Huerta and three Ripple Effect artists - Brandon Garcia, Corey Thomas, and Turner Spring - confirmed their departure from EA on LinkedIn. Catheryn Grant, operations product manager at both Ripple Effect and Respawn, also revealed she was among those impacted, as was EA Motive's senior gameplay designer Jamieson Shearer. Full Circle's senior designer David Milne and seasonal creative director John Epler are affected too.
In a memo to staff shared overnight, EA said it had paused development of an unannounced Sims project called Project Lotus in order to focus on a different title dubbed Project Evergreen. The company also said it was downsizing Full Circle to "create an experience that keeps [players] engaged over the long-term", so there was already some suggestion those studios would face job cuts.
More surprising, though, are the cuts at Respawn, a studio EA said it would be investing "heavily" in to support the growth of free-to-play shooter Apex Legends. Respawn is also co-developing a new project alongside DICE, which is reportedly Star Wars: Battlefront 3. By the same token, EA said it's throwing its "full weight behind" Motive Studio's Iron Man game and Respawn's Star Wars Jedi sequel, its only two action-adventure projects currently in the works.
This is the first round of layoffs at EA since the company was fully acquired by a consortium made up of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, investment firm Silver Lake, and private equity company Affinity Partners earlier this year. The trio acquired EA in the summer for $55bn in one of the largest leveraged buyout deals ever.
When the deal closed, EA told debt investors it would cut $700m in annual costs, including $170m in "organisational efficiencies". At the time, many feared that would translate to major layoffs.

item.title: Microsoft has revealed how much its Xbox cloud gaming service is going to cost, with 50 hours of stream-time selling for an introductory price of $11.99. Read more
item.description:
Microsoft has revealed how much its Xbox cloud gaming service is going to cost, with 50 hours of stream-time selling for an introductory price of $11.99.
This information comes from a post on the official Xbox news website, which explains that starting today, Xbox Insiders will be able to stream games using the paid service without needing an active Game Pass subscription. This comes ahead of a planned rollout to all Xbox players in November. These paid packs provide an ad-free version of the free cloud gaming service revealed earlier this year.
The full suite of introductory prices are as follows:
It's worth noting that even people paying for the Xbox cloud streaming service will encounter wait times during peak hours, though the blog post stated these waits will be shorter.
Microsoft previously revealed that monthly time limits will be placed on its paid Xbox cloud gaming service, though it insisted only a fraction of players would run into this cut-off point. A report claimed a 15-hour cap placed on the Game Pass Ultimate cloud gaming service was present as that's the moment Xbox starts losing money. Offering a cloud gaming service requires server infrastructure, compute costs, and network and bandwidth costs.
As an aside, Sony's defunct cloud gaming service PlayStation Now used to charge $9.99 for a month of streamed game time, more than a decade ago.
Xbox is currently in the midst of a massive restructuring process, in which more than 3,000 employees are to be laid off from the company. In a recent report, additional waves of layoffs are said to be planned for later this month, November, and January.

item.title: A new Star Wars: Battlefront game is reportedly in the works, and it's said to have Apex Legends and Star Wars Jedi studio Respawn working on it, as well as Battlefield and Battlefront developer DICE. Read more
item.description:
A new Star Wars: Battlefront game is reportedly in the works, and it's said to have Apex Legends and Star Wars Jedi studio Respawn working on it, as well as Battlefield and Battlefront developer DICE.
The information comes from "multiple sources" on Variety, and arrives in the wake of EA's sudden decision to lay off 400 workers, close iconic role-playing game studio BioWare, and cancel several projects. As part of a memo to staff, EA executives confirmed that Respawn and DICE are collaborating on a new project, but stopped short of saying what it was.
The report follows days of murmurings from different sources that a third Battlefront game is in the works. It started with a rumour from Electronic Gaming Monthly magazine (via Giant Bomb), which said Disney had been on the lookout for a studio to develop Battlefront 3. The names of potential teams included DICE, and Destiny and Marathon developer Bungie.
Wardogs studio head Joe Brammer then responded to the rumour on X, saying it was actually DICE and Respawn working together on Battlefront 3 - information that now appears to be true.
In 2022, EA was said to have cancelled multiple Star Wars projects in development at the time, including a follow-up to Battlefront 2. That most recent game in the Battlefront series launched in 2017 to a mixed reception. The launch version is mostly remembered for introducing loot boxes to the series that assigned random chance to earning functional in-game characters and powers. It was universally disliked. The backlash was so disastrous it kicked off a wave of legislation worldwide that deemed loot boxes to be gambling mechanics, the fallout of which persists to this day.
DICE would end up overhauling many of those systems and removing loot boxes altogether. The developer turned Battlefront 2's fortunes and player sentiment around, continuing to support the game for years, before releasing its final major update in 2020.
Battlefront 3 would be the first in the series to be published by the now Saudi-owned EA. Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, together with investment firm Silver Lake and private equity company Affinity Partners, acquired EA in the summer for $55bn in a leveraged buyout deal.

item.title: Not only is EA closing down BioWare and cancelling the next Mass Effect - Electronic Arts has now announced a heap of drastic changes that include cutting 400 jobs across the company, pausing development on a project connected to The Sims, and bringing together Respawn and DICE. Read more
item.description:
Not only is EA closing down BioWare and cancelling the next Mass Effect - Electronic Arts has now announced a heap of drastic changes that include cutting 400 jobs across the company, pausing development on a project connected to The Sims, and bringing together Respawn and DICE.
In a memo first sent to staff and later published online, CEO David Tinson and CSO Cam Weber first took a moment to thank employees before letting them know they might lose their jobs.
"Today, we're the number one publisher in Western HD gaming," the duo wrote. "That's an extraordinary position to lead from, and one we should be proud of. Yet our industry is changing quickly. Players have more choices than ever for their time and attention, competition is intensifying, and some of our biggest opportunities for growth are beyond the markets, platforms, and business models where EA has traditionally been the strongest."
The executives then laid out some changes to its portfolio of games. Top of the list is the closure of BioWare, the legendary role-playing powerhouse behind games such as Mass Effect and Dragon Age. Bloomberg reports around 400 jobs will be cut as part of the cost-cutting changes, including roughly 50 job cuts at BioWare.
As for The Sims, the publisher claims it's prioritising something called "Project Evergreen" and is giving "the team more time to reach the full potential and vision for the game." To do so, the execs said they're "pausing development" on another Sims-related title called "Project Lotus." The early access Skate reboot (skate.) has apparently "had a lot of success," but the publisher is still restructuring the studio into a "more focused, smaller team," regardless.
Marvel's Iron Man game (the one that leaked recently) and a third Star Wars Jedi game remain untouched, apparently, though it sounds like we'll see fewer big-budget action-adventure games come from the publisher going forward: "Beyond that, we will concentrate our efforts on fewer simultaneous, large-scale projects, ensuring that every game we build in this space is fully set up for success."
EA also re-emphasised its commitment to Apex Legends and the Battlefield series after the success of Battlefield 6. But that's not all. "We'll be bringing together our Respawn and DICE studios to collaborate on a future project." There's been some rumblings about a possible Star Wars: Battlefront follow-up this week, though EA doesn't give any more concrete details about what this game could be.
Then there's the publisher's golden goose, EA Sports. The executives said they're still committed to FC and the rest of its sport simulations, alongside two new projects that'll be revealed in the next few months - the return of Fight Night and a "brand-new, social-first open-world experience for our American Football team that we call 'Project Gridiron'".
"The decisions we’re making in our priorities, how we work, and with our portfolio reflect our belief in EA’s future. Some open exciting new possibilities. Others are difficult, especially for the people and teams across the company who are directly affected. In those cases, we will support impacted employees in exploring other opportunities within EA, and we're committed to treating impacted colleagues with care and respect," the executives added.
A group of investment firms led by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund took EA private earlier this summer, in a deal worth around $55 billion.

item.title: After over three decades of iconic RPGs, developer BioWare is closing down and its in-development Mass Effect game is no more. The move comes just months after corporate owner EA was bought out by a group of investment firms for $55 billion. Read more
item.description:
After over three decades of iconic RPGs, developer BioWare is closing down and its in-development Mass Effect game is no more. The move comes just months after corporate owner EA was bought out by a group of investment firms for $55 billion.
"For more than 30 years, BioWare has been more than a studio. It has been a home for storytellers, developers, and the players who brought our worlds to life," the role-playing powerhouse wrote on social media this evening before listing some of its greatest hits - Baldur's Gate, Neverwinter Nights, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, Dragon Age, Mass Effect and Anthem.
"Now, after more than three decades of shared adventures, BioWare is closing and early development on the next Mass Effect project is ending. There is nothing easy about writing those words. Our focus right now is on our incredibly talented team who put their hearts into these games, and supporting one another through this transition."
"What generations of BioWare built together is something to celebrate and remember. These games became so much more because you played them, debated your choices, fell in love with the characters, and made these worlds your own. From all of us at BioWare, thank you for being the most meaningful part of our story," the statement continued.
Layoffs at BioWare were expected following EA's acquisition this summer - which saw investment firm Silver Lake, private equity group Affinity Partners (led by Jared Kushner, Donald Trump's son-in-law) and Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund group together and raise $55 billion to buy the publisher. A full studio closure this soon is a surprise, to put it lightly.
A Bloomberg report also claims EA is planning to cut roughly 400 jobs across the company, or around 3 percent of its total workforce. "Across our portfolio, we're making deliberate choices to align talent and investments where we see the greatest opportunities for players and long-term growth," CEO David Tinson and CSO Cam Weber said in a letter to staff seen by Bloomberg.
BioWare itself has been in rough waters these past few years. The studio's live-service experiment Anthem quickly fell from the sky, and its most recent game, Dragon Age: The Veilguard, failed to meet EA's internal sales expectations, leading to another round of layoffs at the developer. Here's hoping the impacted devs can land on their feet soon.
The next Mass Effect game - dubbed Mass Effect 5 by some fans - was seemingly not ready to go into full production. Last we heard, BioWare was trying to reassure folks the game was still definitely in development.

item.title: Developer One More Level is wall-running toward another big success with its recently-released first-person Soulslike, Valor Mortis, which has already broken even after its first week. Read more
item.description:
Developer One More Level is wall-running toward another big success with its recently-released first-person Soulslike, Valor Mortis, which has already broken even after its first week.
The studio best known for shoot-and-slash series Ghostrunner celebrated the milestone earlier today. "We are beyond proud to announce that Valor Mortis has officially reached a break-even point in just seven days," the developer wrote in a recent social media post.
"This incredible milestone wouldn't be possible with you," it added. "Thank you for answering the Emperor's call and believing in our vision!"
We are beyond proud to announce that @ValorMortis has officially reached a break-even point in just 7 DAYS! This incredible milestone wouldn't be possible without YOU. Thank you for answering the Emperor's call and believing in our vision! https://t.co/w0Bh6y2YrO
Breaking even means Valor Mortis has officially made back the money that was spent on its production - every sale from here on out is presumably pure profit for One More Level and the game's publisher, Lyrical Games.
What makes the achievement even more impressive is that Valor Mortis came out in perhaps the most hectic period for new games we've seen in years. The inevitable black hole known as GTA 6 understandably crammed tons of games into the months before and after its November release date - heavy hitters such as Control Resonant, Onimusha: Way of the Sword, Silent Hill Townfall, Gears of War: E-Day, Marvel's Wolverine, and many more launched mere weeks or sometimes even days apart from each other. (Take a look at our upcoming games calendar and you'll see what I mean.)
Still, the historical first-person action game managed to grapple to success largely thanks to a warm reception. Eurogamer's Valor Mortis review praised the ways in which it went above and beyond the typical Soulslike formula. Here's what our Matt Wales had to say: "Valor Mortis is a delight; a gloriously entertaining Soulslike whose fluid foundational combat and cleverly designed enemy encounters would probably be enough on their own. But then One More Level goes further: the exhilarating parkour, the thrilling sense of momentum that shapes everything from the intricate level design and memorable bosses to the sword- and gunplay, elevating it further."
One More Level was also pretty open about releasing a game during such a chaotic time. The developer previously explained that Valor Mortis costs £40/$40 because it knew "this fall is stacked and there's high demand for your time and money." The studio smartly pushed the game out of its original 24th September release date, too, which would've had it going toe-to-to with both Control Resonant and Silent Hill Townfall.
Valor Mortis launched last week across PC, PS5, Xbox Series X/S and Game Pass. When asked about DLC and future patches, the dev simply replied "Working on it!"

item.description:
CD Projekt Red has detailed the substantial update coming to Cyberpunk 2077, revealing a new dual-wielding skill for pistols and revolvers, cyberware customisation, cross-platform mod support, and a brand-new Edgerunners-related story quest featuring voice actors from the Netflix anime show.
The update arrives 22nd October on PC, PS5, and Xbox Series S/X, with the Switch 2 version following "in a couple of days", CDPR media manager Laura Beitzel said during a RedStream this afternoon.
Actual details on the new Edgerunners-related story quest were intentionally thin, but Cyberpunk 2 associate game director Pawel Sasko said it had been written with people involved in the Netflix show, and CDPR publishing producer Natlia Pych it would be a prequel to Edgerunners 2. "It will be the last job of the King's team," Pych said, and it will let us meet characters on the team: Emily, Meshuga, and Miguel.
There'll also be a new Edgerunners radio station added to Cyberpunk 2077 to listen to, which has 16 tracks comprised of songs from both Edgerunners 1 and 2, Sasko said.
Another new type of quest coming in the update is Night City Tours, which is a less action-focused pursuit - the word "cosy" was thrown around. Night City founder Richard Night tells you the lore of the city while things happen around him that don't quite seem to add up. This is a mystery you need to solve. There are also minor tarot arcana being added to the game for you to find, in conjunction with an actual physical deck going on sale.
Cross-platform mod support in Cyberpunk 2077 comes hot on the heels of cross-platform mod support being added to the Remastered update for The Witcher 3, and it works in a very similar way. It's also a partnership with mod platform Mod.io, and there's a panel in the game where you can browse mods - "including the adult mods", Sasko said with a smile - and download and install them. And this is a work in progress: more mods will be added over time.
Implantable cyberware is becoming customisable via new "glam docs" being added to the game alongside - sometimes literally - the ripper docs you already find there. There are five new glam docs dotted around the city, each with their own shop space, and each offering bespoke visual upgrades. This allows you to colour your implants the way you want them.
Beside that, there are a "ton" of new optimisations coming to the game, including a field of vision slider at long last, proper DLSS 4.5 support, and metal frame interpolation and denoising on Mac, whatever that is - it sounded like it was a big deal.
