item.description:
Red Dead Redemption 2's infamous animated horse testicles, which are realistic enough to contract in cold weather and expand again in the warmth, were apparently not a feature mandated by Rockstar. As iconic as they've become - a symbol of extraordinary detail in the game - they didn't originate from a list of features that needed to be added to the game. The horse testicles were instead the unexpected work of one person, or a group of people, autonomously working on the Cowboy epic.
Journalist Jason Schreier heard this anecdote from Rockstar head of development Aaron Garbut while visiting Rockstar North to write an expansive report for Bloomberg about the making of GTA 6. "Garbut actually brought this up," Schreier said in a video on YouTube. "[The horse testicles were] not something that was on some big list of features to make; it was not something that an art director told an artist, 'Alright, we've got to get those horse testicles in here - better put in nights and weekends so you can get these horse testicles in here.'
"That was something that people, or a person on their own, autonomously decided, 'OK, I'm going to do this because I think it's a really cool detail and I have enough time to work on it." We're checking the veracity of this anecdote with Rockstar, by the way.
And that anecdote is important because it relates to another thing Schreier was told by Garbut, which was that no one person at Rockstar knows everything that's in GTA 6 because it's too big and detailed to do that. "There's no one person that has this whole thing in their head," Garbut apparently said.
That, coupled with the fact that developers apparently have "autonomy to put in things that are cool", Schreier said, means there could be another unexpected feature like horse testicles in GTA 6. And given the nudity-related GTA 6 video leaks we've already had, perhaps the features aren't that far removed.
Schreier's video revealed a few other tidbits of information learnt on his trip to Rockstar. He was told that roads in GTA 6 are "significantly narrower" than in GTA 5, apparently, so players feel the effects of traffic more - a detail that relates to the increased levels of realism in GTA 6.
He also heard how some artists had been working on GTA 6 for 11 years, and whereas there were "five of six" people in GTA 5's art production team, there were - or are - 65 people in GTA 6's art production team. Note that Rockstar, as a company, has roughly doubled in size since the release of 2018's Red Dead Redemption 2, growing from 2,441 employees to 4,711 across 12 offices.
There's also some information about the origins of the contextual 'hold left trigger' interaction system introduced in Red Dead Redemption 2, which again, apparently came from someone autonomously working on the game - Phil Hooker (now director of technology) - rather than from one of the game's creative leads. Also, many experiments were apparently done to find a replacement for GTA's radial menu but in the end, the team reverted back to it.
Grand Theft Auto 6 is, of course, releasing a month from now on 19th November. The road to launch has been bumpy, however, with Rockstar North currently embroiled in an employment tribunal in Scotland over the alleged unjust firings of 31 employees, and with a series of gameplay footage leaks exposing GTA 6 in ways that are outside of Rockstar's control.

item.title: Bungie surprised players last month by announcing its intention to bring back Destiny 2 campaigns and other additions taken out of the game over the years. When that 'unvaulting' plan was initially announced, Bungie didn't share any specifics, nor a timeline as to when we can expect the things to return. Read more
item.description:
Bungie surprised players last month by announcing its intention to bring back Destiny 2 campaigns and other additions taken out of the game over the years. When that 'unvaulting' plan was initially announced, Bungie didn't share any specifics, nor a timeline as to when we can expect the things to return.
Now, the developer is finally offering some hints. Bungie head of product, Josh Deane, revealed that Bungie is close to sharing a progress update. "I know there are a lot of questions on the how, what, when of unvaulting. Including any potential future updates to D2 and what's beyond for Destiny," Deane wrote on X in a post only recently spotted by The Game Post. "There's going to be a very intentional process for all of it that will take time."
Deane said Bungie will begin "talking about what our first step is going to look like with more clarity" at the end of October, which we're coming close to now. The Bungie boss also said the development update won't come in the form of a traditional roadmap. Instead, Bungie views it as "a progress bar" the studio hopes will "bring you all closer, more consistently to our dev milestones".
"Just be transparent about any challenges we run into and show you the proof of work along the way that unlocks further understanding," Deane explained. "That way when we share a release date we're all on the same page and have the right expectations that leads directly into how we'll further celebrate Destiny's legacy and vision for the future."
Following the 'unvaulting' Destiny 2 announcement, a Forbes report shed more light on what players can realistically expect from Bungie. The report said that removed campaigns, raids and destinations are coming back, but not expired live seasons. It also suggested that work shouldn't be taken to mean Destiny 2 is back in active development.
In June, Bungie released one final major Destiny 2 update as it announced the end of active development of the shooter-MMO. The update added much-requested features, fixed some longstanding issues and even introduced new things to play. It reignited interest in the game, seemingly enough to convince Bungie to kickstart efforts to bring back deleted content.

item.title: The developers of Umamusume: Pretty Derby have announced a sudden cancellation of an upcoming LA concert, laying the blame on an inability to receive the proper visas despite exploring "every possible option". Read more
item.description:
The developers of Umamusume: Pretty Derby have announced a sudden cancellation of an upcoming LA concert, laying the blame on an inability to receive the proper visas despite exploring "every possible option".
The concert, which was set to take place on the 22nd and 23rd October, offered digital and in-person tickets to fans of the anime horse racing franchise. These tickets are being refunded, though fans remain frustrated.
"Although we have coordinated repeatedly with all parties concerned and explored every possible option in our efforts to make this event happen, we were unable to obtain the necessary visas for entry into the US, so we have come to the painful conclusion that holding the concerts is no longer possible," the announcement message reads.
"To all the Trainers who were eagerly looking forward to the show, we sincerely apologize for the inconvenience and concern this causes, and for announcing this so close to the event date."
For fans who had planned to attend the event in-person, the announcement also notes that options are being explored to help alleviate the frustration, though nothing has been announced at this time. The cancellation announcement ends with another apology to fans, but also the Umamusume cast, company staff, and others involved in the production of the show.
Fans, as you may have guessed, are annoyed. Not at the Umamusume developers or event organisers, but rather the political realities that have led to this outcome. "I've only ever gone to one concert and I was really looking forward to vibing with everyone at the venue and making this my second. I'm not even mad, just disappointed. Cygames will never set foot in America and I don't blame them. Not after all this shit," writes X user Soramoto.
"I’d be so mad if I had to wait six months for a Visa with no response too," writes Reddit user ScorchingDragon. "Feel really bad for the people who planned a trip out to LA though. Now they have to cancel last-minute or find something else to do. At least they can go to cosplay day at Santa Anita racetrack…"
One wonders whether this situation will dissuade Cygames from organising similar events in the US in the future. Elsewhere in the video game industry, concerns surrounding US events have also continued to bubble. A number of game developers and executives expressed concerns about traveling to GDC 2026 due to changes in immigration policy.

item.title: Origame Digital, the studio behind 2020's critically acclaimed Umurangi Generation, has just released a new game but banned it from being sold in Israel. Read more
item.description:
Origame Digital, the studio behind 2020's critically acclaimed Umurangi Generation, has just released a new game but banned it from being sold in Israel.
Penguin Colony is a Lovecraftian horror game experienced through the eyes of a penguin, based on author H.P. Lovecraft's story At the Mountains of Madness. Fellow Traveller, the game's publisher, confirmed that Penguin Colony is not on sale in Israel in a Steam community thread. The thread was created by a Steam user living in Israel wondering if the game had been delisted from Steam.
"While in general we seek to bring our games to as many potential players as possible, we believe strongly that developers have the right to control where their games are sold," Fellow Traveller replied. "In this case, the developer asked us to block sale in Israel. In the absence of more organised sanctions, this act is intended to demonstrate solidarity with Palestine. We fully support their decision."
That message is further reinforced by Penguin Colony itself, which features a post-credits scene that makes clear the studio's stance on Israel's genocide of the Palenstinan people. As shared online, the message reads: "The cowardice of the Games Industry during the ongoing genocide of Palestine by Isreal will be recorded by the art it makes."
Origame Digital has been vocal about its politics, both in and outside of its games, so this latest move is not surprising. Penguin Colony also features a strong land acknowledgement statement at its start.
"This game was made on Wurundjeri Woiwurrung land," it reads. The Kulin Nation never ceded sovereignty to the British Commonwealth. We pay respect to Elders past present and emerging as Indigenous creatives working on land that isn't our own. The land will always be Aboriginal Land no matter what."
In Penguin Colony, you play as a penguin whose home has been invaded by rival human factions searching for an ancient being. You can jump between the different penguins of the colony as you witness and attempt to evade the chaos. The game is currently available on PC, with console editions planned for 2027.
Recently, House House, the studio behind one of this year's most celebrated games, Big Walk, said the game does not have an Xbox version because parent company Microsoft is one of the BDS boycott's targets. Microsoft has ties with the state of Israel that include providing its military with cloud and AI systems used in the ongoing genocide.

item.title: Digital Sun - the indie studio behind moreish roguelike Moonlighter and moody RTS Cataclismo - has delayed a planned Steam playtest for its next game, ReVamp, citing concerns over "games being reverse-engineered, cloned and published before the original is even out." Read more
item.description:
Digital Sun - the indie studio behind moreish roguelike Moonlighter and moody RTS Cataclismo - has delayed a planned Steam playtest for its next game, ReVamp, citing concerns over "games being reverse-engineered, cloned and published before the original is even out."
The developer was planning to let folks into its vampiric "Tower Defensevania" ReVamp near the end of this spooky month, but a new trend of gen-AI copycats cloning both old and unreleased games left the studio worried.
"So many of you signed up for ReVamp's first playtest here on Steam (thank you!), but we've decided to start with something more contained on our Discord, with the public playtest coming a bit later," the developer wrote in a recent Steam blog post.
Digital Sun pointed the finger at "news of games being reverse-engineered, cloned and published before the original is even out," and worried that "sharing a build with tens of thousands of players" months prior to its full launch is "too big a risk."
From here, Digital Sun will grant access to ReVamp's first playtest in waves starting from the 29th of October, via Discord. "Even if you don't get in right away, we'd love for you to join the conversation around ReVamp as we let more players in. We hope to open the public playtest around January. To everyone who requested access here on Steam: we're sorry for the change of plans, and thank you for your patience," the studio added.
ReVamp launches in full on 25th March, 2027. Here's hoping the move can successfully shoo away any would-be clones.
Digital Sun isn't the only developer having to work around the gen-AI boom. Xbox recently announced an entire department that sounds like it's focused on gen-AI game-making, as just one example.
Meanwhile, Alliance Arts outright cancelled a Steam Next Fest demo for its anime-inspired Russian Roulette game, Drunken Goddess Reflux, because of similar issues. "We are concerned that, based on the content of the demo, works imitating or replicating this game's presentation and gameplay could be quickly produced using AI or other tools and released ahead of the game's launch," the company said last week.
Steam Next Fest 2026 should be a great occasion to discover new and exciting games that were previously nowhere near your radar. However, as we reported earlier today, the shadow of generative AI looms over the entire event and could dampen an otherwise great Steam tradition.

item.title: Final Fantasy 7 Revelation will let players access Hard Mode from the very beginning of the journey, unlike FF7 Remake and Rebirth, which made folks roll credits before unlocking the tougher difficulty option. Read more
item.description:
Final Fantasy 7 Revelation will let players access Hard Mode from the very beginning of the journey, unlike FF7 Remake and Rebirth, which made folks roll credits before unlocking the tougher difficulty option.
The tidbit comes courtesy of director Naoki Hamaguchi, who told Hardcore Gamer that Final Fantasy 7 Revelation's Hard Mode "won't function in the exact same way" as it did previously. For next year's third and final chapter, the team "reimagined the high-difficulty experience to align with the new game design."
You see, this time around, the world of Gaia supposedly opens up really early in the game. Cloud and company can fly straight to some of the game's toughest battles as soon as they jump into their flying airship, whether they're ready for the fight or not, so Square Enix's approach to difficulty had to change too.
"Hard Mode is selectable from the very start of this game," Hamaguchi explained. "Therefore, players who want to tackle challenging battles and high-difficulty gameplay right from the beginning can enjoy that experience from their very first playthrough. This is because, unlike Remake and Rebirth, Revelation offers a wide variety of end-game content even after you've beaten the game. Rather than relying solely on the traditional flow of challenging Hard Mode after beating the game, we aimed to create a game where players can enjoy various new content and challenges even after completing the main story."
As much as I loved both Remake and Rebirth, the combat never properly pushed me to my limits and tested my creaky reflexes until I finally reached that second playthrough - in the case of Rebirth, that meant playing the game for at least 50 hours. FF7 Revelation is shaping up to be another behemoth that could easily take 100 hours to fully complete, apparently, so I'm very relieved to hear that I can get to the good stuff from the jump. Hard Mode is truly where these games shine.
In a separate tweet, Hamaguchi also shared there'll be a Dynamic Mode at launch, like in Rebirth, "allowing players to enjoy consistently challenging battles throughout the game." It also looks like we'll be able to adjust how tricky those many, many mini-games are. (Damn you, Moogles!)
Final Fantasy 7 Revelation is coming to PC, PS5, Nintendo Switch 2 and Xbox Series X/S on 8th April, 2027.

item.title: Arc Raiders is still going strong almost a year after finding viral success, and it's all thanks to Embark Studios' one-two-punch strategy of launching a huge new update, Frozen Trails, to coincide with a free weekend. Read more
item.description:
Arc Raiders is still going strong almost a year after finding viral success, and it's all thanks to Embark Studios' one-two-punch strategy of launching a huge new update, Frozen Trails, to coincide with a free weekend.
Arc Raiders' Frozen Trails update upgraded the extraction shooter to version 2.0 earlier this month - 8th October - and quickly led to a surge in Steam players interested in its tense PvEvP shootouts. A new report from Alinea Analytics' Rhys Elliott now claims a similar resurgence took place across all platforms where the game's available.
According to the report, Arc Raiders' comeback peaked with a whopping 1.7m daily players jumping in on the 14th of October, its biggest player count in six months, mostly driven by the aforementioned update. What's perhaps most interesting is that player numbers actually peaked just after the game's free trial weekend ended on 12th October - though around 150,000 new looters reportedly joined the robo-infested wasteland during that weekend period.
Both events coincided with the game's steepest discount yet, slashing its price tag by 50% to $19.99. In the three days after the free trial, Arc Raiders sold another 150,000 copies and brought home roughly $3m, not counting microtransactions, per the report.
Embark Studios' seemingly went all out this month. Frozen Trails itself nudged almost every corner of the game, adding a new map, new weapons, new menacing mechs and much more.
A PvE test also tried to accommodate the game's surprisingly friendly community between the 13th and 20th of October. Executive producer Aleksander Grøndal recently said the team isn't against the idea of permanently splitting Arc Raiders' PvEvP gameplay into PvE and PvP pockets. Who knows? Doing so could open the door to another resurgence if done well.
Earlier this month, we learned the production company behind this summer's big screen horror hit, Backrooms, is working to adapt both Arc Raiders and The Finals into film and TV projects. Developer Embark is involved, too.
